messageValues.message:
You get the column names of a spreadsheet of sales leads, each with a few sample values. People name their columns in many ways and in any language. Say which columns hold each piece of information.

For each field, return the list of column names that hold it, copied exactly as written. Usually it is one column, sometimes several, and an empty list when no column holds it.

- email: the lead's email address.
- first_name: the person's first name only.
- full_name: the person's full name, when there is no column with just the first name.
- company: the name of the business.
- website: the business website or domain.
- role: the person's job title or position.

Look at the sample values, not only at the names. Ignore every column whose name starts with "Outreach" or "Follow-up".

You write cold emails from one person (the sender) to one stranger (the lead). The lead has never heard of the sender and gets sales emails every day. The email must read like a note the sender typed for this one person, never like marketing.

You get the sender's OFFER BRIEF, what the sender's list says about the lead, and text from the lead's website.

# FACTS
- Everything about the sender comes from the OFFER BRIEF: who they are, their clients, results, numbers, the offer, the guarantee, the ask and the sign-off. Use its exact numbers. Never invent or change a client, a result, a number or a guarantee. If the brief has no proof, write the email without proof.
- Everything about the lead comes from the list and the website. Never state something you cannot see there. Never claim the sender is a customer, a fan or a follower of the lead, and never claim they have met.
- Respect what the brief says the emails must never say.

# THE EMAIL
Four parts, in this order. Each one answers the next question in the reader's head.

1. Opener: "Is this spam?" One sentence, two at most. Greet the lead by first name, then make one real observation about their business, the kind a person notices after a minute on their website: what they sell, who they serve, where they work, something they announce. The opener is only about them: the sender does not appear in it, so it never starts with "I work with", "I help" or anything the sender does. With no website, use what the list says about them ("saw you run a roofing company in Phoenix"). Plain and casual. It must not sell or hint that a pitch is coming. Do not quote their slogan, do not praise their mission, values or passion, and do not mention details so specific that it sounds like a machine read the page. If you have nothing specific, write a short honest line about their kind of business instead of faking it.

2. Who I am: "Who are you and why should I care?" One or two sentences. Introduce the sender through proof: the client or result in the brief that looks most like this lead.

3. Offer: "What can you do for me?" Two or three sentences. First an observation about a problem or missed opportunity that a business like theirs very likely has. Then the offer from the brief: the specific result, the timeframe, and what happens if it is not delivered or why saying yes costs them nothing. One number, never a range. No prices.

4. Ask: "How do we proceed?" One sentence with the single ask from the brief. One step, never two questions.

Then the sign-off from the brief, on its own line. Nothing after it.

# VOICE
- One person to one person. Say "I", not "we", unless the brief speaks as a team.
- Short sentences, plain words, contractions. Write the way people text a business contact they respect.
- Say names the way people say them out loud: first name only, and the company without Inc, LLC, Ltd or similar. Never put a name in quotes or in capitals.
- Not allowed: "I hope this email finds you well", "I came across", buzzwords, long dashes, emojis, bullet lists, bold, links, placeholders in brackets, a P.S., more than one exclamation mark.
- The email body has 60 to 130 words, in short paragraphs separated by a blank line.

# SUBJECT
2 to 5 words, lowercase, with the lead's first name or company. It sounds like a note from someone they might know and makes them curious. It never sells, never states the offer and never uses the word "quick".

# FOLLOW-UP
A second email, sent a few days later only if the lead has not replied. One to three short sentences: a casual ping in the same voice that recalls the offer in a few words and repeats the ask. It has its own subject, different from the first one, 2 to 4 words, lowercase, never with the word "quick". No subject ever starts with "Re:" or "Fwd:".

# LANGUAGE
Write in the language the brief asks for. If it does not say, use the language of the lead's website, or English.

# FIELDS
- subject, body: the first email. The body starts with the greeting and ends with the sign-off.
- follow_up_subject, follow_up_body: the follow-up, also ending with the sign-off.
- opener_based_on: a few words saying which fact the opener uses and where it comes from (website, list, or general).

parameters.content:
## Write and send personalized cold emails with follow-ups using AI, Google Sheets and Gmail

Turn a list of leads into cold emails that sound written by hand. AI reads each lead's website and writes the email and a follow-up.

### How it works
1. **Start Outreach** is the main way in. Put your leads in your Google Sheet and click Execute workflow: it handles the next leads with no status.
2. **Add One Lead** is a form for a single lead. **Import Leads File** takes a CSV or Excel file. Both save the leads in your sheet first, then run the same steps.
3. Your columns can have any names: AI finds the email, name, company and website. Only the email is required, but role and notes make better emails.
4. Each email follows a proven 4-part structure, is checked against fixed rules, then saved as a Gmail draft or sent.
5. The workflow adds its own columns to your sheet. **Outreach Status** shows each lead's stage: Drafted, Sent, Needs review, Replied or Followed up.
6. Run it again days later: leads who did not reply get the follow-up.

### Setup
- [ ] Create a Google Sheet, with your leads or empty. It is always required: every lead and its status is stored there.
- [ ] Write your offer brief in a Google Doc: paste [this interview prompt](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Ihfll_Fc6Xnr18ds4IPTbOyGLGOkeBHiYQ6Ytu-ZjFo/edit?usp=sharing) into any AI chat and save its answer.
- [ ] Paste both links in **Outreach Settings**.
- [ ] Connect Gmail, Google Sheets, Google Docs and Gemini.
- [ ] Click **Execute workflow**. Activate only to use the forms.

### Customization
Switch `send_mode` to `send` when you trust the drafts. Use any chat model instead of Gemini. Swap Start Outreach for a Schedule Trigger to run daily.

## 1. Three ways to start
Start Outreach works through the leads already in your sheet. The two forms add leads to the sheet first, then run the same steps.

## Set these first
Your sheet link and your offer brief link.

`send_mode`: `draft` or `send`.
`emails_per_run`: leads handled each run.
`follow_up_after_days`: `0` turns follow-ups off.

## 2. Understand the list
AI matches your column names to email, name, company and website. Then the next leads are picked, up to your limit.

## 3. Research and write
Reads each lead's website and writes the email and its follow-up from your offer brief.

## 4. Quality check
Fixed rules, no AI: length, links, spam phrases, placeholders. A failed email is rewritten once.

## 5. Follow up
Looks for a reply in Gmail. No reply means the follow-up goes out.

## 6. Send and log
Sends or saves a draft, then writes each lead's stage in the Outreach Status column, with the date and the email.
